en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sahadhammika-vagga 79.
The Training Rule on Counteracting Karma.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six monks, having engaged in improper conduct, protested whenever an individual formal act was being performed against them.
On another occasion, when the Saṅgha had assembled for some business,
the group of six monks, while engaged in robe-making, gave their consent (*chanda*) to one person.
Then the Saṅgha, thinking, "Friends, this bhikkhu of the group-of-six has arrived alone; come now, let us perform a formal act against him," performed a formal act against him.
Thereupon, that bhikkhu went to where the bhikkhus of the group-of-six were.
The group-of-six monks said to that monk,
“Friend, what has the Saṅgha done? “Friends, the Saṅgha has performed a formal act against me.”
“Friends, we did not give our consent for this purpose,
thinking, ‘He will do your work.
And if we had known that he would do your work, we would not have given our consent.”
Those monks who were few in desires... they complained, grumbled, and protested:
“How can the group-of-six monks, having given their consent for legal acts, subsequently engage in the practice of criticizing them? ... [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that you gave your consent for legal acts and subsequently engaged in the practice of criticizing them?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, having given your consent for legal acts that are in accordance with the Dhamma, later fall into the state of criticizing them?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘If any monk, having given his consent for formal acts that are in accordance with the Dhamma, should afterwards fall into a state of grumbling, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever such a person...
"a monk."
... [as before] ... this is the meaning of "bhikkhu" intended here.

A "legitimate" (dhammika) legal act (kamma) is one performed according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction—namely, an act of notification (apalokanakamma), an act consisting of a motion (ñattikamma), an act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma), or an act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatutthakamma). This is what is called a legitimate legal act.
If, having given his consent, he reviles [the assembly], it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, in a legitimate legal act (dhammakamma), perceiving it as a legitimate legal act, he gives his consent and then reviles [the assembly], it is an offense of expiation.
If, in a legitimate legal act, being doubtful about it, he gives his consent and then reviles [the assembly], it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
If one perceives an illegal act as an illegal act and, having given consent, censures it, there is no offense.
If one perceives an illegal act as a legal act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one is uncertain regarding an illegal act, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and he perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is no offense.

There is no offense if he reviles [the monks] while knowing: "An illegitimate procedure has been performed, or it was performed by an incomplete assembly, or it was performed on one who does not deserve a legal procedure."
[It is] for one who is insane,
for a first-time offender.
The ninth training rule on obstructing an act is finished.
